title: I need assistance with balancing a hobby rpg maker mv project inspired by Early FFXI and OSRS. (Turn based, fantasy theme)

posts.author: vilereaver41
posts.body:
Grind, that's is the word I'm looking for, I need a damage formula that is going to not bloat stats but make the player work for their keep but not make then insane. I don't want them to steam roll every mob unless they are 10-20 levels above it.
In terms of the mix between game types I wanted items to hold meaning and not be tossed away after being replaced, a wood sword could be used for a crafting recipe that in turn can also be used for something else.
I do have status effects and states, but my struggle atm is enemy and weapon balancing. Currently I have enemys up to level 35, I am most likely going to cap things at 45-50 levels for the moment. I'm just worried my enemys will be to strong or to weak, as my player advances and uses items.
I want the player to feel everything has meaning and not to throw away a single thing.
Current weapons
These have icons already ingame and their stays with status effects to.
Enemy sheet
The last set of enemys have no stats, I have not messed with their ex parameters or their abilitys to give them anything unique.
I don't like stat bloat as I intend to increase level cap as I am happy with content to a certain level, but balancing is making me crazy. HELPPP!!

posts.author: SGHarlekin
posts.body:
There's only one solution: Playtest, playtest, and then playtest some more until it feels just right for each and every enemy. There's no magic formula that just balances your game for you.
Playtest every combination of enemies the player encounters at any given point in time with gear setups the player is likely going to have at the time of the encounter. Playtest with sub-optimal setup, playtest with overleveled setup. Playtest some more with a combination of items and then playtest some more for good meassure.

posts.author: Andar
posts.body:
There are ways to reduce the neccessary playtests, but you'll never forgoe them.
and if you go that route, you basically replace some playtests with a lot of mathematics.
One trick is to start from the opposite end.
You decide how long a battle should last, and how much HP both the enemy and the player have to loose - in the case of the player a partial number of the full HP if the player is to win.
This will determine how much average damage each action should do to the other side - HP divided by number of turns in entire battle.
Then you think about the skills and the damage formula (something basic like the default formula, nothing fancy) and that leads to the attack and defense values your actors and enemies need to have with their skills to get to that average damage.
Next step would be to determine how the actor gets those values as part of the base values for the expected level and what equipment is available.
and only after that you playtest if the numbers work out correctly despite the several shortcuts you took and assumptions you made.

While balancing a game is an unavoidable task, there are several strategies to simplify the process. For instance, using flexible formulas rather than fixed parameters can help, as you mentioned.
Another approach is to write code that allows the game to play itself and record the results and details of battles. There are also many other tips to consider.
